result.summary: A short headnote explains that Megakles of Athens won a Pythian victory in 490 B.C. and belonged to the Alkmaionidai. Pindar then opens by praising Athens and the family, lists their victories, and notes that envy follows success.

scenes.title: Editor's note on Megakles
scenes.summary: The editor gives the date of the victory and the family background of Megakles.

scenes.title: Praise of Athens and envy
scenes.summary: Pindar hails Athens and the Alkmaionidai, recounts their victories at the games and the temple at Pytho, and laments the envy that good fortune brings.
scenes.stakes: Megakles' fame is threatened by the envy that follows great success.

notable_quotes.reason: A famous opening praising Athens as the fairest prelude of song.

analysis.text: The ode celebrates family glory and the city of Athens, while acknowledging that envy accompanies success.
The victory dates to 490 B.C., the year of Marathon, and the Alkmaionidai were a powerful Athenian family. The temple at Delphi they rebuilt is the glorious house in sentence 6.

fun_facts.text: This is among Pindar's shortest odes and is noted for praising Athens, which was also the subject of other celebrated Pindaric lines.

language_notes.text: "Fairest of preludes" means the best possible opening for a song; a prelude is the introductory part of a choral ode.
"Citizens of Erechtheus" means the Athenians, named for Erechtheus, an early legendary king of Athens.
The "glorious house" is Apollo's temple at Pytho (Delphi), rebuilt with Alkmaionid money after a fire.
Kirrha was the port of Delphi, so victories "at Kirrha" are Pythian victories won in the games there.
"Requiteth" means repays; envy repays noble deeds with spite instead of thanks.
"Fair hap" is good fortune; "engender bad with good" means lasting prosperity breeds trouble alongside it.

context_notes.text: The Battle of Marathon in 490 B.C. was the Athenian victory over the Persian invasion force.
Kleisthenes reformed Athens' government around 508 B.C.; Perikles, the later statesman, was descended from the family through his mother.
The Isthmian, Olympic and Pythian games were major Greek festivals. Olympia honoured Zeus, and Pythian games honoured Apollo.

literary_notes.text: Pindar opens by praising Athens itself as the finest starting point, tying the city's glory to the family's praise.
The question implies no place or house is more glorious, flattering Athens and the Alkmaionidai without stating it.
Envy is made an agent that repays noble deeds, turning the victor's success into a cause of Pindar's own sorrow.
